scenes.narration: Those who met Ulysses S. Grant at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Grant (born Hiram Ulysses Grant; April 27, 1822 – July 23, 1885) was the 18th president of the United States, serving from 1869 to 1877, and was the Commanding General of the Union Army. Grant was born in Ohio and graduated from the United States Military Academy in 1843.

The private years of Ulysses S. Grant explain the public decades better than any speech. He served with distinction in the Mexican–American War, but returned to civilian life impoverished in 1854. In 1861, shortly after the Civil War began, Grant joined the Union Army.

The family Ulysses S. Grant came from matters more than the legends admit. In 1863, he led the Vicksburg campaign that gave Union forces control of the Mississippi River and dealt a major strategic blow to the Confederacy. President Abraham Lincoln promoted Grant to lieutenant general and command of all Union armies after his victory at Chattanooga.

The first real success of Ulysses S. Grant arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Lee through the Overland Campaign, which ended when Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox. In 1866, President Andrew Johnson promoted Grant to General of the Army.

The last chapter of Ulysses S. Grant was written long after the fame. A war hero, drawn in by his sense of duty, Grant was unanimously nominated by the Republican Party and elected president in 1868. As president, Grant stabilized the post-war economy, supported Reconstruction and the Fifteenth Amendment, and prosecuted the Ku Klux Klan.

The whole life of Ulysses S. Grant reads like a single decision repeated. An effective civil rights executive, Grant signed a bill to create the United States Department of Justice and worked with Radical Republicans to protect African Americans. Grant was re-elected in the 1872 presidential election, but was inundated by executive scandals during his second term.

Between the birth and the legend of Ulysses S. Grant lie the years that actually decide it. His response to the Panic of 1873 was ineffective in halting the Long Depression, which contributed to the Democrats winning the House majority in 1874. In his foreign policy, the Alabama Claims against Britain were peacefully resolved, but the Senate rejected his proposal to annex Santo Domingo.

The reputation of Ulysses S. Grant was built in the middle, not at the edges. During the disputed 1876 presidential election, he facilitated the approval by Congress of a compromise. Leaving office in 1877, Grant undertook a world tour, becoming the first president to circumnavigate the world.

Somebody like Ulysses S. Grant should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. In 1880, he was unsuccessful in obtaining the Republican nomination for a third term. In 1885, dying of throat cancer, Grant wrote his memoirs, which were posthumously published and became a major critical and financial success.

The life of Ulysses S. Grant begins far from where the story usually starts. At his death, he was the most popular American and was memorialized as a symbol of national unity. Due to the pseudohistorical and negationist mythology of the Lost Cause of the Confederacy spread by Confederate sympathizers around the turn of the 20th century, historical assessments and rankings of Grant's presidency suffered considerably before they began recovering in the 21st century.

Ulysses S. Grant was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Grant's father, Jesse Root Grant, was a Whig Party supporter and a fervent abolitionist. He and Hannah Simpson were married on June 24, 1821, and their first child, Hiram Ulysses Grant, was born on April 27, 1822.

To understand where Ulysses S. Grant ended up, start with where Ulysses S. Grant began. To honor his father-in-law, Jesse named the boy "Hiram Ulysses", though he always referred to him as "Ulysses". In 1823, the family moved to Georgetown, Ohio, where five siblings were born: Simpson, Clara, Orvil, Jennie, and Mary.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Ulysses S. Grant ran through years nobody filmed. At the age of five, Ulysses started at a subscription school and later attended two private schools. In the winter of 1836–1837, Grant was a student at Maysville Seminary, and in the autumn of 1838, he attended John Rankin's academy.

Each stage of the life of Ulysses S. Grant made the next stage possible. In his youth, Grant developed an unusual ability to ride and manage horses; his father gave him work driving supply wagons and transporting people. Unlike his siblings, Grant was not required to attend church by his Methodist parents.

The people who knew Ulysses S. Grant young describe someone already restless. For the rest of his life, he prayed privately and never officially joined any denomination. Hamer nominated Ulysses to the United States Military Academy at West Point, New York, in spring 1839.

What Ulysses S. Grant built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Initially, Grant was indifferent to military life, but within a year he reexamined his desire to leave the academy and later wrote that "on the whole I like this place very much". Seeking relief from military routine, he studied under Romantic artist Robert Walter Weir, producing nine surviving artworks.

By the time Ulysses S. Grant reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. On Sundays, cadets were required to march to services at the academy's church, which Grant disliked. Quiet by nature, he established a few intimate friends among fellow cadets, including Frederick Tracy Dent and James Longstreet.

The rise of Ulysses S. Grant was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. He was inspired both by the Commandant, Captain Charles Ferguson Smith, and by General Winfield Scott, who visited the academy to review the cadets. Grant graduated on June 30, 1843, ranked 21st out of 39 in his class and was promoted the next day to brevet second lieutenant.

Setbacks came early for Ulysses S. Grant, and the response to them is the real story. He would later write that among the happiest days of his life were the day he left the presidency and the day he left the academy. Despite his excellent horsemanship, he was not assigned to the cavalry, but to the 4th Infantry Regiment.

The legacy of Ulysses S. Grant outlived the circumstances that produced it. Grant was happy with his commander but looked forward to the end of his military service and a possible teaching career. In 1844, Grant accompanied Frederick Dent to Missouri and met his family, including Dent's sister Julia.

Few lives travel as far as that of Ulysses S. Grant, and the distance is the point. On August 22, 1848, they were married at Julia's home in St. Grant's abolitionist father disapproved of the Dents' owning slaves, and neither of Grant's parents attended the wedding.

The childhood of Ulysses S. Grant contains the adult in small print. Grant was flanked by three fellow West Point graduates in their blue uniforms, including Longstreet, Julia's cousin. The couple had four children: Frederick, Ulysses Jr. ("Buck"), Ellen ("Nellie"), and Jesse II.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Ulysses S. Grant — in that order. After the wedding, Grant obtained a two-month extension to his leave and returned to St. Louis, where he decided that, with a wife to support, he would remain in the army.

The turning point in the life of Ulysses S. Grant looked like a failure at the time. Grant's unit was stationed in Louisiana as part of the Army of Occupation under Major General Zachary Taylor. Polk ordered Taylor to march 150 miles (240 km) south to the Rio Grande.

Every biography of Ulysses S. Grant has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Marching to Fort Texas, to prevent a Mexican siege, Grant experienced combat for the first time on May 8, 1846, at the Battle of Palo Alto. Grant served as regimental quartermaster, but yearned for a combat role; when finally allowed, he led a charge at the Battle of Resaca de la Palma.

The education of Ulysses S. Grant happened mostly outside any school. He demonstrated his equestrian ability at the Battle of Monterrey by volunteering to carry a dispatch past snipers; he hung off the side of his horse, keeping the animal between him and the enemy. Polk, wary of Taylor's growing popularity, divided his forces, sending some troops (including Grant's unit) to form a new army under Major General Winfield Scott.

What Ulysses S. Grant wanted at the start and what Ulysses S. Grant got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Traveling by sea, Scott's army landed at Veracruz and advanced toward Mexico City. For his bravery at Molino del Rey, Grant was brevetted first lieutenant on September 30.

The defining trait of Ulysses S. Grant was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. At San Cosmé, Grant directed his men to drag a disassembled mountain howitzer into a church steeple, then reassembled it and bombarded nearby Mexican troops. On September 14, 1847, Scott's army marched into the city; Mexico ceded the vast territory, including California, to the U.S. on February 2, 1848.

Those who met Ulysses S. Grant at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. During the war, Grant established a commendable record as a daring and competent soldier and began to consider a career in the army. He studied the tactics and strategies of Scott and Taylor and emerged as a seasoned officer, writing in his memoirs that this is how he learned much about military leadership.

The private years of Ulysses S. Grant explain the public decades better than any speech. In retrospect, although he respected Scott, he identified his own leadership style with Taylor's. Grant later believed the Mexican war was morally unjust and that the territorial gains were designed to expand slavery.

The family Ulysses S. Grant came from matters more than the legends admit. Historians have pointed to the importance of Grant's experience as an assistant quartermaster during the war. Although he was initially averse to the position, it prepared Grant in understanding military supply routes, transportation systems, and logistics, particularly with regard to "provisioning a large, mobile army operating in hostile territory", according to biographer Ronald White.

The first real success of Ulysses S. Grant arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Grant came to recognize how wars could be won or lost by factors beyond the battlefield. Grant's first post-war assignments took him and Julia to Detroit on November 17, 1848.

The last chapter of Ulysses S. Grant was written long after the fame. He was soon transferred to Madison Barracks, a desolate outpost in upstate New York in need of supplies and repair. After four months, Grant was sent back to his quartermaster job in Detroit.
